lesson.title: Under the Microscope: Social Anxiety Disorder
lesson.summary: Social anxiety disorder is a marked, persistent fear of social situations driven by concern about being negatively judged by others, going well beyond ordinary shyness or nervousness.
lesson.body:
Social anxiety disorder involves marked fear or anxiety about one or more social situations in which a person might be scrutinized by others, whether that means having a conversation, being observed doing something, or performing in front of people. The core fear is not simply about the situation itself but about being judged: the person is afraid that they will act in a way, or show visible signs of anxiety, that will be seen as embarrassing, humiliating, or offensive to others, or that will lead to rejection. To meet the diagnosis, these situations must almost always provoke fear, be avoided or endured only with significant distress, be clearly disproportionate to the actual social risk involved, and persist for six months or more while causing meaningful impairment.

It is worth distinguishing this from ordinary nervousness, since almost everyone feels some anxiety before a job interview or a big presentation. What separates social anxiety disorder from that common experience is intensity, persistence, and breadth: the fear is severe enough, frequent enough, and disruptive enough that it shapes major choices, such as avoiding classes that require speaking up, turning down promotions that involve meetings, or struggling to order food at a restaurant because a server might be listening.

There is a useful connection between social anxiety disorder and how psychologists study stereotypes and social judgment more broadly. A great deal of research on stereotypes examines what happens when people believe others are watching them through a critical or unflattering lens, for instance the anxiety and performance cost that can come from fearing you will be seen as confirming a negative stereotype about a group you belong to. Social anxiety disorder involves a related, though more generalized and more personal, version of that dynamic: an intense, chronic fear of being negatively evaluated as anxious, awkward, or incompetent by whoever happens to be present, regardless of any specific group identity. In both cases, the anticipation of being judged through an unfavorable lens can itself become distressing and self-perpetuating, since worrying about how one will be perceived can make a person appear more visibly anxious, which then feeds the very fear of negative evaluation that started the cycle.
